stimulus: An astronomy student models light from a distant star as two parallel rays, line $\ell$ and line $m$. The edge of a telescope mirror lies along line $t$, which crosses line $\ell$ at point $P$ and line $m$ at point $Q$. At point $P$, the angle between line $t$ (going from $P$ toward $Q$) and line $\ell$ (going to the right of $P$) measures $58^\circ$. At point $Q$, the angle between line $t$ (going beyond $Q$, away from $P$) and line $m$ (going to the left of $Q$) measures $x^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Line $t$ cuts parallel lines, so the corresponding angle at $Q$, between line $t$ going beyond $Q$ and line $m$ going to the right, is also $58^\circ$. Angle $x$ sits on the other side of line $m$ and forms a linear pair with that angle, so $x = 180 - 58 = 122$.

A.why: You treated lines $t$ and $m$ as perpendicular and took $90 - 58$. The question never says there is a right angle.

B.why: You found the corresponding angle at $Q$ and stopped there. Angle $x$ is the angle next to it on the straight line, so you still have to subtract it from $180$.

D.why: You added $90$ and $58$, as though $x$ were made of a right angle plus the given angle. Nothing in the figure supports that sum.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $ABC$?
stimulus: On a site plan for an excavation, two straight survey lines, $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BE}$, cross at point $C$. Points $A$, $B$, and $C$ form a triangle. The measure of angle $BAC$ is $47^\circ$, and the measure of angle $DCE$ is $68^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Angles $DCE$ and $ACB$ are vertical angles, so angle $ACB$ also measures $68^\circ$. The angles of triangle $ABC$ add up to $180^\circ$, so angle $ABC = 180 - 47 - 68 = 65^\circ$.

A.why: You subtracted the two given angles ($68 - 47$) when you needed to subtract both of them from $180$.

C.why: $68^\circ$ is angle $ACB$, which you get from the vertical-angle step. It is a corner of the triangle, but it isn't angle $ABC$.

D.why: You found the angle that forms a straight line with angle $ABC$ ($180 - 65$). The question asks for the interior angle at $B$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $PRS$?
stimulus: A printmaker carves a triangular block $PQR$. Side $\overline{QR}$ is extended past $R$ to point $S$. At vertex $Q$, sides $\overline{PQ}$ and $\overline{RQ}$ are both extended past $Q$, and the angle between those two extensions measures $71^\circ$. The measure of angle $QPR$ is $44^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: The angle between the two extensions at $Q$ is vertical to angle $PQR$, so angle $PQR = 71^\circ$. Angle $PRS$ is an exterior angle of triangle $PQR$, so it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles: $44 + 71 = 115^\circ$.

A.why: $65^\circ$ is the interior angle $PRQ$ ($180 - 44 - 71$). Angle $PRS$ is the exterior angle beside it, so you needed $180 - 65$.

B.why: $71^\circ$ is angle $PQR$, which you get from the vertical-angle step. It is at vertex $Q$, not at $R$.

D.why: You took $180 - 44$ and never used the $71^\circ$ angle at $Q$. The exterior angle at $R$ depends on both opposite interior angles.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $JLM$?
stimulus: A linguist sketches a triangular diagram $JKL$ to compare three related dialects. In the diagram, $JK = JL$ and angle $KJL$ measures $40^\circ$. Side $\overline{KL}$ is extended past $L$ to point $M$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Since $JK = JL$, the base angles at $K$ and $L$ are equal, and each one measures $\frac{180 - 40}{2} = 70^\circ$. Angle $JLM$ forms a straight line with angle $JLK$, so it measures $180 - 70 = 110^\circ$.

A.why: You took $90 - 40$, as if the triangle had a right angle. The diagram gives you equal sides, not a right angle.

B.why: $70^\circ$ is the interior base angle $JLK$. Angle $JLM$ is the exterior angle next to it on line $KM$.

D.why: You found the supplement of the apex angle at $J$ ($180 - 40$). That is the sum of the two base angles, not the exterior angle at $L$.

stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of angle $BAC$?
stimulus: A sports scientist marks two parallel lines on a sprint track, line $\ell$ and line $m$. Point $A$ lies on line $\ell$. Points $B$ and $C$ lie on line $m$, with $B$ to the left of $C$. Point $D$ lies on line $\ell$ to the left of $A$. The measure of angle $DAB$ is $62^\circ$, and the measure of angle $ACB$ is $50^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
explanation: Lines $\ell$ and $m$ are parallel and $\overline{AB}$ crosses both of them, so the alternate interior angles $DAB$ and $ABC$ are equal, which makes angle $ABC = 62^\circ$. In triangle $ABC$, angle $BAC = 180 - 62 - 50 = 68^\circ$.

A.why: $62^\circ$ is angle $ABC$, which you get from the parallel-line step. You stopped before using the triangle sum to find the angle at $A$.

C.why: $62 + 50 = 112$ is the exterior angle of the triangle at $A$, next to angle $BAC$. It isn't angle $BAC$ itself.

D.why: You took $180 - 62$, as though angles $DAB$ and $ABC$ added up to $180^\circ$. They are alternate interior angles, so they are equal.
